tasks.q: Write a presence check: refuse a sign-in name that has not actually been typed.
brief: Read one line of text.
Spaces on their own do not count as a name, so ignore any spaces at the start and end.
If nothing is left, print: no name given
Otherwise print: welcome followed by a space and the name, with those outer spaces removed.
tasks.starter: # Read a name and check that something was really typed

tests.why: An ordinary name should be accepted and printed back after the word welcome.
Pressing enter with nothing typed is the empty string, and that is the case a presence check exists for.
Four spaces look like nothing on screen but are not the empty string - strip them before you test for empty.
The name is real but padded. Strip it once and use the stripped version, or the stray spaces end up in your output.

tasks.fb: A presence check means checking the input is not empty once the spaces around it have been removed.

tasks.q: Write a type check that refuses anything that is not a whole number.
brief: Read one line of text.
It only counts as a whole number if every character is a digit - a minus sign or a decimal point means it is not.
If it is a whole number, print: number: followed by a space and the number.
Otherwise print: not a number
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Read a line and decide whether it is a whole number

tests.why: Digits only, so this is a whole number and the number itself is printed after the label.
Letters are not digits. Calling int() on this straight away would crash the program, which is what a type check prevents.
Nothing typed at all is not a whole number either - isdigit() is False for the empty string.
A decimal point is not a digit, so this fails the check even though it is a number.
The brief says digits only, and a minus sign is not a digit - so this one is refused here on purpose.
Zero is a perfectly good whole number. A check that tests whether the number is true rather than whether it is digits would reject it.

tasks.fb: isdigit() asks the question safely, before int() gets the chance to crash.

tasks.q: Write a range check for a satisfaction score from 1 to 10 inclusive.
brief: Read one whole number.
If it is from 1 to 10 inclusive, print: valid
If it is below the range, print: too low
If it is above the range, print: too high
tasks.starter: # Read a score and check it is from 1 to 10 inclusive

tests.why: An ordinary score comfortably inside the range.
1 is the bottom boundary and inclusive means it is allowed - if you got too low you used < 2 or <= 1 the wrong way round.
10 is the top boundary and is allowed. This is where < and <= get confused.
One below the boundary, so it must be refused. 0 is the value a range check most often lets through by mistake.
One above the boundary. Testing > 10 rather than >= 10 is what makes this one work.
Well below the range, and still too low rather than too high.

tasks.fb: Inclusive means both boundaries pass, so the four values worth testing are 0, 1, 10 and 11.

tasks.q: Check a temperature that may be negative, and refuse anything that is not a number.
brief: Read one line of text.
A minus sign at the front is allowed here, but a decimal point is not.
If it is not a whole number, print: not a number
Otherwise, if it is from -5 to 35 inclusive, print: ok
Otherwise print: out of range
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Read a temperature, which may be negative, and check it

tests.why: An ordinary reading inside the range.
The bottom boundary is negative, so isdigit() on its own cannot accept it - this is where try and except earn their place.
One step below the boundary. With negatives it is easy to write the comparison the wrong way round.
The top boundary is inclusive and must be accepted.
One above the top boundary, so out of range.
A word cannot be turned into a number, so int() raises an error that must be caught instead of crashing.
int() refuses a decimal point too, so this is reported as not a number rather than rounded.

tasks.fb: try and except around int() catch the wrong type; the range test then runs only on a value you know is a number.

tasks.q: Write a length check for a password that must be from 8 to 16 characters.
brief: Read one line of text, exactly as it is typed.
If it is fewer than 8 characters, print: too short
If it is more than 16 characters, print: too long
Otherwise print: ok
tasks.starter: # Read a password and check its length

tests.why: Ten characters is inside the range, so this one passes.
Seven characters is one short of the minimum, so it must be refused.
Exactly 8 characters is allowed - if this prints too short you used <= 8 instead of < 8.
Exactly 16 characters is the top boundary and is still allowed.
Seventeen characters is one over the maximum, which is the boundary a length check usually misses.
Nothing typed has length 0, which is fewer than 8 - so too short, not a crash.

tasks.fb: len() gives the length; the two boundaries worth testing are 7 and 8 at one end, 16 and 17 at the other.

tasks.q: Write a format check for a booking reference: two letters then four digits.
brief: Read one line of text and ignore any spaces at the start and end.
A valid reference is exactly 6 characters: the first two must be letters, the last four must be digits.
Capital or small letters are both fine.
If it matches, print: valid reference
Otherwise print: invalid reference
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Read a booking reference and check it is two letters then four digits

tests.why: Two letters then four digits, so this is the shape the check is looking for.
Small letters are allowed, so isalpha() is the right test rather than comparing against the capitals.
Only five characters. Check the length first, or slicing a short string quietly gives you a shorter piece and the check passes.
Seven characters. A check that only looks at the first six characters would let this through.
The second character is a digit, not a letter, so the letters part fails.
The third character is a letter, so the four digits are not all digits.
Nothing typed must be refused rather than crash - the length test catches it before any slicing matters.

tasks.fb: A format check is a length check and a check on what each part contains, and both have to pass.

tasks.q: Keep asking for a lift number until a valid one is typed.
brief: The building has lifts 1 to 5.
Read a whole number.
If it is not from 1 to 5 inclusive, print: please enter 1 to 5 - and read another one.
Keep going until a valid number is typed.
Then print: lift followed by a space and the number.
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until the lift number is from 1 to 5

tests.why: A valid number first time needs no message at all - do not print the warning before you have checked.
One bad go, one message, then the good one is accepted. A loop that only checks once would accept the 9.
It has to keep asking however many times it takes, and 5 is the top boundary so it is allowed.
1 is the bottom boundary. If this prints a warning, your condition is refusing the value it should accept.
6 is one over the top. Reading the next number inside the loop is what gives the user another go.

tasks.fb: The usual shape is to read once, then a while loop that prints the message and reads again while the value is still wrong.

tasks.q: Keep asking for a two-digit house number, and say which rule was broken each time.
brief: Read one line of text at a time.
If it is not a whole number made only of digits, print: that is not a whole number
Otherwise, if it is not from 10 to 99 inclusive, print: that is outside 10 to 99
Either way, read another line and try again.
When a valid number is typed, print: accepted: followed by a space and the number.
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Keep asking until a valid two-digit house number is typed

tests.why: Valid straight away, so the only line printed is the acceptance.

out: that is not a whole number
tests.why: A word is the wrong type, so the type message comes first - checking the range before the type would crash here.
Both 9 and 100 are the right type but outside the range, and 10 is the bottom boundary so it is accepted.

out: that is not a whole number
that is not a whole number
tests.why: Nothing typed and a decimal both fail the type check, and 99 is the top boundary so it is accepted.
0 is digits, so it gets the range message and not the type message.

tasks.fb: Check the type first and the range second, because a range test on text that is not a number is what crashes the program.

tasks.q: Write a sign-in check against a small list of accounts.
brief: The two lists are written for you - do not change them. A username and the password in the same position belong together.
Read a username on the first line and a password on the second.
If the username is not in the list at all, print: unknown user
If the username is there but the password does not match exactly, print: wrong password
If both match, print: access granted
Capital and small letters are different, so the match must be exact.
tasks.starter:
users = ['hpatel', 'lokoye', 'mdiaz']
passwords = ['Fern2041', 'Kite9183', 'Vole5570']

# Read a username and a password, then check them against the lists

tests.why: Both halves match, so access is granted. Make sure you compare against the password in the same position as the username.
A different account must work the same way - a program that only ever checks the first user fails here.
Only the first letter differs in case, and that is still a different password - do not lower() the password before comparing.
A real username with another user's password must be refused, so the two checks have to be tied together.
No such username, so the answer is unknown user even though the password belongs to somebody.
The username is in capitals and the brief says the match is exact, so this counts as an unknown user.

tasks.fb: Find the username first; only once you know where it is can you look up the password that belongs with it.

tasks.q: Allow three attempts at a passcode, then lock the account.
brief: The correct passcode is written for you - do not change it.
Read a passcode and compare it exactly.
If it is right, print: access granted - and stop asking.
If it is wrong, print: wrong passcode - and let the user try again.
Allow three attempts in total. If all three are wrong, print: account locked - and do not ask a fourth time.
tasks.starter:
passcode = 'Owl4472'

# Allow three attempts, then lock the account

tests.why: Right first time, so nothing else is printed - no warning and certainly no lock.
One wrong go then the right one. The loop must stop as soon as it is right, not use up all three attempts.
Any wrong passcode gets the same message, and the second attempt still works.
The third attempt is still allowed, so this must be granted rather than locked.
Three failures lock the account. If your program asks for a fourth passcode it will run out of input and crash.
A passcode in the wrong case is wrong, so the first attempt fails - passwords are case sensitive.

tasks.fb: Count the attempts and stop on either condition: three used up, or the right passcode given.

tasks.q: Keep asking for a username, then an age, until each one is valid.
brief: First read usernames until one is valid, checking in this order:
if it is fewer than 5 or more than 12 characters, print: username must be 5 to 12 characters
otherwise if it is not made only of letters and digits, print: username must be letters and digits only
Then read ages until one is valid, checking in this order:
if it is not made only of digits, print: age must be a whole number
otherwise if it is not from 11 to 19 inclusive, print: age must be 11 to 19
Ignore spaces at the start and end of what is typed.
Finally print: registered followed by a space, the username, a space and the age.
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Ask for a username until it is valid, then an age until it is valid

tests.why: Both valid first time, so the only line printed is the registration.
Four characters is one short, five is the boundary and allowed, and 11 is the bottom of the age range.
Twelve characters is the top boundary for the username and 19 the top of the age range, so both are accepted.
Thirteen characters is one over the top and fin9 is one under the bottom, so both get the length message - the loop has to keep asking after each one.

out: username must be letters and digits only
username must be letters and digits only
tests.why: A space and a hyphen are both long enough but neither is a letter or a digit, so the second rule catches them.

out: age must be a whole number
age must be a whole number
tests.why: Nothing typed and a word both fail the type check; 10 and 20 are one outside each end of the range.

tasks.fb: Each rule gets its own message and the checks go in order, so the user is told the one thing that is actually wrong.

tasks.q: Write a defensive stock-taking program that keeps going when a line of data is wrong.
brief: Read lines until the line done is typed.
Each line should be an item name, a comma, then a quantity. Ignore spaces at the start and end of the name and the quantity.
Check each line in this order:
if it does not have exactly one comma, print: bad line
otherwise if the quantity is not made only of digits, print: bad quantity
otherwise if the quantity is not from 1 to 99 inclusive, print: out of range
otherwise count it, add the quantity to a running total, and print: added followed by a space and the item name.
A wrong line must not stop the program - carry on with the next one.
When done is reached, print: accepted: followed by a space and how many lines were added.
Then on the next line print: total: followed by a space and the total quantity.
The program must not crash on any input.
tasks.starter: # Read lines until 'done', checking each one and carrying on after a bad line

tests.why: Two good lines, so both are added and the total is the two quantities added together.
No data at all is not an error - the counters start at 0 and both are printed.
No comma and two commas are both bad lines, and neither may stop the program.
A quantity in words must be reported rather than passed to int(), which would crash the whole run.
0 and 100 are one outside each boundary; 1 and 99 are the boundaries themselves and are allowed.
The spaces round the name and the quantity must be stripped, or the name prints padded and the digit check fails.

tasks.fb: Defensive design means a wrong line is reported and skipped, not allowed to stop the whole run.

tasks.q: Which kind of check is each rule?
items: The field has not been left empty
The value is a whole number
The reading is a number, not a word
The reference is two letters then four digits
The date is written as DD/MM/YYYY
tasks.fb: A length check counts characters; a format check tests the pattern they make.

info.title: Strip it first
info.text: A stray space is still a character, so a presence check should strip the input before testing it for empty.

info.title: Inclusive means both
info.text: 'From 1 to 10 inclusive' means 1 and 10 both pass. Test them: that is exactly what boundary data is for.

info.title: Length, then format
info.text: Checking the length first means a format check can safely look at a particular position in the string.

info.title: Three tries
info.text: Locking an account after three wrong passwords stops a program being guessed at one attempt at a time.

info.title: Never stored plainly
info.text: Real systems never keep a password as it was typed. They store a hash of it, which cannot be read back.

info.title: Keep going
info.text: A program that skips a bad line and says how many it skipped is more useful than one that stops at the first problem.
